faqs: Can I refuse to disclose my current CTC?

You can politely say you prefer to discuss what the role is worth, but in India most employers expect the figure and may verify it later. Refusing can slow the process or create doubts. Usually it is better to share it and steer the discussion towards your expected range.
What documents will they ask for to verify CTC?

Common requests include recent payslips, your current offer or increment letter, Form 16 and bank statements showing salary credits. Practices vary, so check with HR. Keep these ready before you reach the offer stage.

items.question: How do I negotiate a job offer?
items.title: How to Negotiate a Job Offer in India (With Scripts)
items.description: Negotiate salary and offer terms politely with research and clear asks. Scripts for freshers and experienced hires, plus what is usually negotiable.
items.why_asked: Negotiation is expected for most lateral hires and is sometimes possible even for freshers off campus. When an employer makes an offer, they have already decided they want you, so a polite, well-reasoned request rarely causes an offer to be withdrawn. What interviewers and HR assess here is how you handle a professional negotiation: whether you are prepared, reasonable and collaborative, or aggressive and unclear. This is the same skill many finance roles require with customers and partners, so your approach also signals how you will behave on the job.
how_to_answer: Thank them and express genuine interest before discussing numbers.
Ask for time to review the full offer, including fixed pay, variable pay, joining bonus, benefits, location and notice buyout.
Make one clear, researched ask with a reason, such as market data, a competing offer or a specific skill you bring.
Consider non-salary items if the budget is fixed: joining date, a review after six months, relocation support or a notice buyout.
Confirm everything agreed in writing before resigning from your current job.

samples.answer: Thank you for the offer; I am genuinely excited about the role and the team. I have reviewed the details, and I wanted to discuss the fixed component. Based on my research and the scope of the role, which includes managing a portfolio of [size], I was expecting fixed pay closer to [₹X] lakh. Is there any flexibility to move closer to that figure? If the fixed budget is limited, I would be happy to discuss a joining bonus or an earlier salary review instead.

I want to be open with you. I have another offer at [₹X] lakh CTC for a similar role. Your company is my first preference because of the role and growth path. If you can come closer to that figure, I would be ready to accept and give my resignation this week.

Thank you very much for the offer. I am keen to join. I understand fresher salaries are usually standard, so I wanted to ask whether there is any flexibility, or whether a review after the probation period is possible based on performance. Either way, I am happy to accept.

mistakes: Accepting the first offer without reading the full break-up.
Bluffing about competing offers that you do not have.
Negotiating aggressively or issuing ultimatums.
Resigning before receiving the final offer letter in writing.
follow_ups: What is the minimum figure you would accept?
Can you join earlier if we increase the offer?
Why should we pay above our band?
faqs: Can freshers negotiate salary in campus placements?

Campus offers are usually standard packages, and negotiating is generally not expected or possible. Off-campus fresher roles sometimes have slight flexibility. Even if salary is fixed, you can politely ask about joining dates, location preference or training details.
Will negotiating make the company withdraw the offer?

A polite, reasonable request rarely leads to withdrawal. The risk increases if you are aggressive, make unrealistic demands or keep changing your ask. Make one well-reasoned request, be clear about what would make you accept, and respond quickly once they reply.

items.question: What is your notice period?
items.title: What Is Your Notice Period? How to Answer in Interview
items.description: Explain your notice period, buyout options and earliest joining date clearly. Sample answers for 30, 60 and 90-day notice periods in Indian jobs.
items.why_asked: Notice periods in India commonly range from 30 to 90 days, and longer notice can be a real obstacle when an employer needs someone soon. The interviewer is checking your earliest realistic joining date, whether you can negotiate an early release, and whether you will honour commitments to your current employer. They also listen for honesty: candidates who promise immediate joining and then cannot get released create problems. A clear, accurate answer with any flexibility you genuinely have helps the hiring manager plan.
how_to_answer: State your contractual notice period exactly, as written in your appointment letter or HR policy.
Mention any flexibility: leave balance you can adjust, a buyout option or the possibility of early release.
Give a realistic earliest joining date and avoid overpromising.
Show professionalism by mentioning that you will complete a proper handover.

samples.answer: My notice period is 90 days, as per my appointment letter. My company does allow early release in some cases if the handover is complete, and I also have about fifteen days of leave balance that may be adjustable, subject to approval. Realistically, I could join in about 60 to 75 days. If you need me sooner, I would be open to discussing a buyout, but I would want to complete a proper handover first.

My notice period is 30 days. Once I receive your offer letter, I will resign the same week. I expect to finish my handover in that period, so I can join within about a month. I do not anticipate any delay, since my manager is aware I am looking for a larger role. I will prepare a handover note for my pending files during the notice period so that my team is not left with gaps when I leave.

I have already resigned, and I am serving my notice period. My last working day is [date], so I can join from [date]. My relieving letter will be issued on my last day, and I can share it with you then. I have already handed over most of my files to my replacement, so there is no risk of my current employer extending my last date.

mistakes: Saying you can join immediately when your notice period is 90 days.
Suggesting you might leave without serving notice.
Not knowing your own notice period or buyout policy.
Overcommitting to an early date without checking with your employer.
follow_ups: Can you negotiate an early release?
Will your current company make a counter-offer?
Would you consider a notice buyout?
faqs: What is a notice period buyout?

A buyout means paying your current employer, or having your new employer pay, salary for the remaining notice days so you can leave early. Whether it is allowed depends on your employer's policy and your contract. Check with HR and get any arrangement in writing.
Can I leave without serving my notice period?

Leaving without serving notice or settling it can lead to withheld dues, problems with your relieving letter and issues in background checks. It also damages your professional reputation. Always discuss options like early release or buyout with your employer instead.

items.question: Why are you asking for such a big salary hike?
items.title: Why Do You Expect a High Hike? How to Justify It
items.description: Justify a large salary hike with market data, added responsibility and skills. Sample answers for job switchers and professionals moving to bigger roles.
items.why_asked: When your expected salary is well above your current CTC, the employer wants to know whether the jump is justified or just ambitious. They are checking whether you understand market rates, whether the new role carries genuinely more responsibility, and whether you can defend your position with facts rather than emotion. Your tone matters too: calm reasoning suggests professionalism, while defensiveness or arrogance does not. A good answer gives two or three solid reasons and leaves room for discussion.
how_to_answer: Explain that your current CTC may be below market, if true, and why (for example, a small organisation or limited increments).
Point to the higher responsibility of the new role, such as a larger portfolio, team or geography.
Mention specific skills or results that add value, like certifications, target achievement or process improvements.
Stay open to discussion, and consider how the total package is structured, not just the fixed pay.

samples.answer: I understand the hike looks large on paper. My current CTC is lower than the market rate for my experience because I have been at a small firm where annual increments have been limited. Over the last two years, my work has grown significantly: I now independently handle [responsibility]. This role also includes managing a team, which I am not doing now. My expectation is based on what similar roles in the market are paying, but I am open to discussing how we structure the package.

The role you are offering is a step up from mine. I would move from handling a single branch's customers to covering a region with [number] branches and reporting to the zonal head. That is a significant increase in responsibility and travel. My expectation reflects that. I have consistently met my targets over the last three years, which I can show through my appraisal letters.

My expectation reflects the specialised skills this role needs. I have [certification or experience] and hands-on experience with [system or process], which is not common in the market. I am confident this will reduce your training time and help me contribute quickly. I am happy to walk you through specific situations where I used these skills, so you can judge whether the expectation is fair.

mistakes: Saying 'everyone gets this much when switching' without reasons.
Revealing personal financial needs like loans as the main reason.
Refusing to discuss or adjust your expectation.
Exaggerating responsibilities or results.
follow_ups: What if we offer a smaller hike with an early review?
What is your minimum acceptable figure?
Do you have another offer at this level?
faqs: What is a typical hike when switching jobs in India?

It varies widely by industry, role, demand for your skills and your current pay. There is no fixed rule, so avoid quoting a standard percentage. Research similar roles and focus on what the new role is worth rather than a hike percentage on your current pay.
Should I mention personal reasons like an EMI for needing a higher salary?

Generally no. Salary discussions should be based on the value you bring and the market rate for the role. Personal financial pressures, while real, do not usually influence the employer and can make you seem less focused on the job.

items.question: Would you accept a lower salary than you expected?
items.title: Would You Accept a Lower Salary? How to Respond
items.description: Respond professionally when an employer offers less than you asked. Sample answers that keep the door open, plus what to ask for instead.
items.why_asked: This question usually means the employer likes you but has a budget constraint, or is testing how firm your expectation is. They want to know whether you are flexible, whether you are genuinely interested in the role beyond money, and where your real floor is. Answering 'yes, anything is fine' weakens your position; answering 'no' too fast may end the conversation. A balanced answer shows interest, asks about the full package and growth path, and states clearly the conditions under which you would accept.
how_to_answer: Do not answer immediately with yes or no; ask what figure they have in mind and how the package is structured.
Know your walk-away figure in advance, based on your expenses, current pay and market research.
Explore alternatives: an early salary review, joining bonus, higher variable pay, or other benefits.
If the role is genuinely valuable for your career, say so, and accept only if the terms still work for you.

samples.answer: I am really interested in this role, so I am open to discussing it. Could you share the figure you have in mind and how the fixed and variable parts are structured? If the fixed component is lower than what I expected, I would appreciate a salary review after six months based on performance. If that is possible, I can be flexible.

samples.who: Career switcher (accepting lower pay for a new field)
samples.answer: Yes, I expected that moving into equity research might mean starting at a lower level than my current IT salary. I have planned for that. What matters more to me is the learning and the growth path. Could you tell me how salary progression usually works for associates after the first year?

I appreciate your openness. I am very keen on the role, but I would not be able to accept below [₹X] lakh CTC, since that is close to my current package and the move involves relocating to a costlier city. If there is any way to reach that figure, through a joining bonus or relocation support, I would be happy to proceed. I would rather be upfront about this now than accept and feel unsettled later, because I want to commit fully to this role.

mistakes: Agreeing immediately to any reduction without understanding it.
Rejecting outright without exploring alternatives.
Accepting a figure you cannot live with and resenting it later.
Not getting agreed conditions, like an early review, in writing.
follow_ups: What is your absolute minimum?
Would a higher variable component work for you?
How soon could you join if we agree?
faqs: Is it wise to take a pay cut for a better role?

It can be, if the role offers significantly better learning, brand value or growth, and you can manage your expenses. It is a personal decision. Think about where the role will take you in two to three years, not just the immediate salary.
How do I ensure a promised salary review actually happens?

Ask for it to be mentioned in the offer letter or a written email from HR, with the timeline and basis for the review. Verbal promises are easily forgotten when managers or policies change. A written confirmation protects both you and the employer.

items.question: What questions should I ask about CTC, in-hand salary and variable pay?
items.title: CTC vs In-Hand Salary: What to Ask Before Accepting
items.description: Understand CTC, in-hand salary and variable pay before accepting an offer. Questions to ask HR, with worked examples for Indian finance job offers.
items.why_asked: Many freshers accept an offer quoting a CTC of, say, ₹6 lakh and are surprised when the monthly credit is much lower. CTC includes items you do not receive monthly, such as employer PF contribution, gratuity provision, insurance premium and performance-linked variable pay. When HR discusses the offer, they also notice whether you understand these components. Asking clear, informed questions shows maturity and protects you from misunderstandings that often lead to early resignations.
how_to_answer: Ask for the full salary break-up: basic, HRA, special allowance, employer PF, gratuity, insurance and variable pay.
Clarify variable pay: how it is calculated, how often it is paid, and what percentage people typically receive.
Estimate your in-hand salary after employee PF, professional tax and income tax deductions, or ask HR for an indicative figure.
Check one-time items like joining bonuses separately, including any clawback if you leave early.
Ask about benefits outside CTC, such as medical cover for family, that add real value.

samples.who: Fresher (questions to HR at the offer stage)
samples.answer: Thank you for the offer. Could you please share the detailed break-up of the CTC? I want to understand how much is fixed monthly salary and how much is variable or annual. Also, how is the variable component decided, and how often is it paid? It would help if you could give an approximate monthly in-hand figure after PF and tax deductions.

I want to compare the offers properly. In your offer, the CTC is [₹X] lakh, but about 20 per cent appears to be variable. Could you tell me how the variable has paid out for this role in recent years? Also, is the joining bonus included in CTC, and is there a clawback if I leave within a year? That will help me make a fair comparison.

Suppose an offer says ₹6 lakh CTC. If it includes ₹60,000 variable, around ₹21,600 employer PF and about ₹14,400 for gratuity and insurance, the fixed gross is roughly ₹5 lakh, or about ₹42,000 a month. After employee PF and professional tax, the in-hand may be around ₹38,000 to ₹40,000 before income tax. Actual figures depend on the employer's structure and current tax rules.

mistakes: Assuming CTC divided by twelve is your monthly salary.
Not asking how variable pay is calculated or paid.
Comparing offers only by CTC without seeing the break-up.
Ignoring clawback clauses on joining bonuses.
follow_ups: Is the variable pay guaranteed in the first year?
Is gratuity part of CTC here?
Which tax regime should I choose?
faqs: Why is my in-hand salary so much lower than CTC?

CTC includes employer contributions like PF and gratuity that you do not receive monthly, variable pay paid later, and sometimes insurance premiums. Your monthly salary is also reduced by employee PF, professional tax and income tax. HR can usually provide an indicative in-hand figure.
Which tax regime gives higher in-hand salary?

It depends on your income and deductions, and rules change with each Budget. As of 2026, check the latest slabs on the income tax department's website or ask a qualified advisor. Your employer will usually ask you to declare your choice at the start of the year.

items.question: What will you do if your current employer makes a counter-offer?
items.title: Counter-Offer From Your Employer? How to Answer
items.description: Answer the counter-offer question in interviews and decide how to handle one. Sample answers and the factors to weigh before staying or leaving.
items.why_asked: Recruiters ask this because candidates sometimes accept a new offer only to use it as leverage, then stay after their current employer raises their pay. This costs the hiring company time and effort. The interviewer wants reassurance that you are moving for genuine reasons, such as role, learning or growth, which a salary increase alone would not fix. Your answer also shows how thoughtfully you make career decisions. A clear statement of your reasons for moving, and how you would handle a counter-offer professionally, builds trust.
how_to_answer: Restate your main reasons for leaving, which should be about the role and growth, not just money.
Say honestly that you would politely decline a counter-offer if those reasons are not addressed by money alone.
Avoid sounding dismissive of your current employer; show respect for their effort to retain you.
Think through your own answer before resigning, so you are not swayed in the moment.

The reason I am moving is the larger scope and the regional responsibility your role offers, which my current employer cannot match in the near future. faqs: Is it a good idea to accept a counter-offer?

It depends. If your reasons for leaving were only about pay, a counter-offer might solve them. But if the issues are about role, growth, manager or culture, a raise rarely fixes them. Also consider that your current employer now knows you were looking to leave. Weigh this carefully.
How do I decline a counter-offer politely?

Thank your manager sincerely for the offer and for their support. Explain briefly that your decision is based on a career move, not salary, and that you have committed to the new role. Offer to complete a thorough handover. Keep the tone positive to preserve the relationship.
